How to Use the Pinterest Trends Tool to Plan Content

By Marie Glow StudioPublished October 9, 2026

The Pinterest Trends tool, free at trends.pinterest.com, helps you plan content by showing how interest in a search term has risen and fallen over time. It lets you compare up to four terms at once and works best when you publish new pins four to six weeks before a trend's peak, not after it arrives.

What Is the Pinterest Trends Tool?

The Pinterest Trends tool is a free research page at trends.pinterest.com that charts how search interest in a term has moved over the past months, as a line on a graph rather than a single number. Type in a phrase and the tool draws a curve showing where interest has been rising, falling or holding steady on Pinterest, so you can see a trend's shape instead of guessing at it from memory or last year's calendar.

This is different from the live suggestions that drop down under Pinterest's own search bar as you type, which answer a narrower question: what related phrases are people searching right now. If you have not already read the guide to Pinterest's search bar autocomplete, that tool and this one answer two different planning questions and work well side by side.

How Do You Compare Terms in Pinterest Trends?

Pinterest Trends lets you start with one search term, then add up to three more, for four terms total sitting on the same graph. That comparison view is where the tool earns its place in a content calendar, because it turns a guess between two ways of phrasing the same idea into something you can actually look at.

A shop could compare a singular and a plural version of a product term, a seasonal name against a generic one, or two near-synonyms a customer might type. Whichever line sits higher, or rises earlier, is the phrase worth building a board, a pin title and a pin description around for that stretch of the year. The comparison does not hand you an exact count of searches. It shows which of your options is the stronger bet, which is enough to decide where to put your time.

How Far Ahead of a Trend Should You Publish?

Publish new pins roughly four to six weeks before a trend's expected peak, based on where the graph shows interest starting to climb in a past year. That lead time exists because a new pin needs room to be seen, saved and clicked before the moment people are actually searching for it arrives, and a pin published the week a trend peaks has already missed most of its own run-up.

Reading the graph for this is straightforward: look at the shape of the curve from a prior year, find the point where the line first turns upward, and count back from the peak. If a term climbs for about five weeks before it tops out, that is your publishing window for the next time the same season comes around. The timeline will not be identical every year, so treat the graph as a planning guide, not a fixed date on a calendar.

How Is Pinterest Trends Different from Pinterest Keyword Research?

Pinterest Trends answers a timing question, when interest in a phrase is rising or falling, while keyword research answers a wording question, which exact phrase to put in a title, description or board name. The two jobs work together rather than replacing each other: Trends tells you which weeks matter for a topic, and keyword research tells you what to actually say once you decide to show up for it. For the wording side of the work, the guide to free and low cost Pinterest keyword research tools and the walkthrough on finding long tail keywords on Pinterest cover that half in more depth.

How Can a Service Business Use Pinterest Trends to Plan Content?

A salon, a contractor or a coach has fewer products to pin than a shop does, but the same timing logic still applies to the services on offer. A salon can check how interest in a seasonal color or style name moves before building a pin and board around it. A contractor can check whether searches tied to a seasonal project, like outdoor lighting or a specific kind of remodel, climb earlier in the year than expected, and plan pins pointing at a quote form accordingly. A coach or consultant can compare a few ways people might search for the problem they solve and build content around whichever phrasing the graph favors for the time of year clients are actually searching.

None of this requires a product catalog. It only requires picking a handful of terms tied to what the business already offers and checking, a few times a year, whether interest in them is about to rise.

What Are the Limits of the Pinterest Trends Tool?

Pinterest Trends shows a relative curve of interest over time, not an exact number of searches, a ranking position or a guarantee that a pin published in the right window will perform. It is a timing signal to plan around, not a scoreboard. Results after using it still depend on the account, the pin itself, the niche and how consistently new pins keep going up, the same honest limits that apply to any Pinterest work.

Checking a graph is also only useful if the rest of the account, boards, pin titles, descriptions and where each pin links, is already working. The Pinterest SEO Audit, $197, reviews whether a business's existing pins and boards already line up with what it sells, as one part of a ranked 30 day action plan, which is a reasonable next step if trend timing alone is not moving the needle.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Pinterest Trends tool the same as the search bar's autocomplete suggestions?

No. Autocomplete shows related phrases people are searching for right now, while Pinterest Trends charts how interest in a term has moved over time so you can see when to plan around it.

How many search terms can Pinterest Trends compare at once?

Up to four: the term you start with, plus three more added to the same graph.

Does Pinterest Trends show the exact number of people searching a term?

No. It shows a relative curve of rising and falling interest, not a raw search count, so it works as a timing signal rather than a scoreboard.
